analysis.one_liner: Requires big meatpackers to publish their cattle contracts and buy a minimum share of cattle through open bidding.
analysis.headline: The bill died without a vote: it sat in a House Agriculture subcommittee from May 2022 until the Congress ended in January 2023, despite a bipartisan sponsor group.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would force the largest cattle slaughterhouses to file their standard contracts with the Department of Agriculture and publish them in a public library, so ranchers can see the premiums, discounts, and terms packers offer before they sell. It would also require the very largest packers — those slaughtering 5% or more of the nation's fed cattle — to buy a set minimum share of cattle through open negotiation or public trading platforms rather than private formula deals, with fines up to $90,000 per week for violations. The aim is to restore real price discovery in a market where a handful of packers dominate buying.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent cattle ranchers and feedlot operators, who sell into a market where a few big packers control most purchases. Today, much of the cattle trade happens through private formula contracts that use negotiated prices as a base — and packers have little reason to bid openly. A public contract library and minimum open-market purchases would give sellers more information and more bidders, which could also push down costs for grocery shoppers.

how_it_helps.text: USDA must build a public library of every type of contract between packers and producers for fed cattle, including schedules of premiums and discounts, contract duration, and how many cattle each contract commits, published in a monthly report.

USDA must create five to seven regions covering the continental United States and set a mandatory minimum share of cattle each large processing plant must buy through approved, openly priced mechanisms — negotiated purchases, negotiated grid purchases, stockyards, or open bidding platforms.
The rules apply to 'covered packers' — those that slaughtered on average 5% or more of the nation's fed cattle over the prior five years — which concentrates the burden on the largest processors.
Packers that violate the minimums face civil penalties of up to $90,000 per violation, with each week of a continuing violation counted as a separate violation.
The bill adds prior-day reporting of 14-day delivery schedules, expedited daily carcass weight reporting, and annual cutout yield reporting to give the market more timely price information.

analysis.who_pays: The largest meatpacking companies, which would have to file contract details with the government, publish terms they now keep private, and shift a set share of purchases back into open bidding — plus the cost of compliance and potential fines.

drawbacks.text: Mandated open-market buying could raise packers' procurement costs, and packers argue such mandates can add costs that flow through to consumer beef prices; the bill itself requires a cost-benefit analysis and notice-and-comment rulemaking before minimums are set.

The bill does not set the actual minimum percentages — USDA sets them by rule, based on average negotiated trade in each region from 2020 through 2022 and capped at 50%, so the real-world effect depends on rules written after passage.

Formula contracts would remain legal; the bill requires a minimum share of open trade but does not ban the private arrangements that dominate the market, so price discovery would improve only by degrees.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The compliance cost on packers is real but modest relative to the value of functioning price discovery in a market where a handful of buyers set prices that anchor the whole cattle trade. The design is careful — region-by-region minimums, a 50% cap, rulemaking with public input, and a chance to cure shortfalls — which trades some speed for durability. The main honest criticism is that it nudges rather than forces: packers keep most formula contracts as long as they hit their negotiated-trade floor.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2022 and sent to the House Agriculture Committee, which passed it along to its livestock subcommittee — and no one ever brought it up again; it died there when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Cynthia Axne (D-IA) introduced the bill on May 3, 2022, joined as original cosponsors by three fellow Iowa Republicans — Reps. Feenstra, Hinson, and Miller-Meeks — and Rep. Hartzler (R-MO).
It was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture the day it was introduced, then on May 19, 2022 to the Subcommittee on Livestock and Foreign Agriculture.
Nine members cosponsored the bill in total: 5 Democrats and 4 Republicans.
No markup, hearing vote, or floor action followed; the bill's last recorded action is the May 19, 2022 subcommittee referral, and the Congress ended January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest beef packers came out ahead: with no law passed, they avoided mandatory contract disclosure and required minimums of open-market buying, keeping their existing formula arrangements intact. Independent ranchers gained nothing from the bill they had bipartisan support for.

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat sponsored the bill and four of its nine cosponsors were Republicans, including three fellow Iowa Republicans; the bill died in committee without a roll call, so no recorded vote shows where the parties stood.

industries.note: The bill targets packers slaughtering 5%+ of national fed cattle, requiring them to publish contract terms and buy a minimum share through open negotiation with fines up to $90,000 per week. Their current advantage — buying most cattle on private formula contracts anchored to prices they have little incentive to bid up — is what the bill was designed to shrink.

industries.industry: Independent cattle ranchers and feedlot operators
industries.note: A public contract library and minimum open-market purchases would give sellers more information and more competing bids when they sell. Because the bill failed, they keep negotiating against concentrated buyers without it.
